title: How SSDs Work
description: Understand NAND flash physics, page/block/plane hierarchy, write amplification, TRIM, SSD endurance, and why random writes are expensive even on flash storage.

segments.text: SSDs changed everything about storage performance, but they're not magic. Understanding NAND flash internals explains why write amplification kills SSD lifespan, why random writes are still expensive, and why the TRIM command matters for sustained performance. This knowledge is critical for database tuning.

NAND flash stores data by trapping electrons in floating gate transistors. A charged gate reads as zero, uncharged as one. SLC stores one bit per cell, MLC stores two, TLC stores three, QLC stores four. Each additional bit reduces endurance dramatically: SLC handles 100,000 write cycles, QLC only 1,000.

Flash has a physical hierarchy. Pages are typically 4 to 16 kilobytes — the minimum read and write unit. Blocks contain 128 to 256 pages — the minimum erase unit. Planes group blocks for parallel operations. Dies contain planes, and multiple dies make a package. This hierarchy creates the fundamental write problem.

Here's the critical constraint: you can write to empty pages, but you cannot overwrite a page in place. To modify data, you write new data to an empty page and mark the old page as invalid. When the block fills up, the controller must erase the entire block — all 256 pages — even if only one page changed. This is the root of write amplification.

Write amplification factor, or WAF, is the ratio of data actually written to flash versus data the host intended to write. A WAF of 3 means for every gigabyte you write, the SSD internally writes three gigabytes. High WAF kills SSD lifespan and reduces write throughput. Random small writes can push WAF above 10.
segments.thought_prompt: Why would random small writes cause higher write amplification than sequential large writes?

segments.text: The SSD controller runs garbage collection continuously. It selects blocks with many invalid pages, copies valid pages to new blocks, then erases the old blocks. This is background work that competes with your foreground I/O. Under sustained heavy writes, garbage collection can't keep up, and write latency spikes from microseconds to milliseconds.

When a filesystem deletes a file, the SSD doesn't know those pages are free. TRIM tells the SSD controller which pages are no longer needed, allowing proactive garbage collection. Without TRIM, the controller must do read-modify-erase-write cycles on blocks that contain only stale data. Always enable TRIM in production — it's discard in fstab on Linux.

SSD endurance is measured in DWPD — drive writes per day over the warranty period. An enterprise SSD might have 3 DWPD for five years: you can write three times the drive capacity daily for five years. A consumer QLC drive might have 0.3 DWPD. For a database with heavy writes, the difference between 3 DWPD and 0.3 DWPD is the difference between years and months of life.

Enterprise SSDs reserve 10 to 28 percent of capacity as overprovisioned space. This spare area gives the garbage collector room to work without blocking foreground writes. It also provides replacement cells for worn-out ones. Consumer drives typically reserve only 7 percent, which is why their performance degrades more as they fill up.

NVMe SSDs bypass the SATA bottleneck entirely. SATA supports one command queue with 32 commands. NVMe supports 65,535 queues with 65,536 commands each. On a modern NVMe drive, random 4K reads deliver 500,000 to one million IOPS with sub-100 microsecond latency. That's 200 times faster than a spinning disk.

Here's why this matters for databases. RocksDB uses LSM trees that generate heavy sequential writes during compaction. PostgreSQL generates random writes during page updates. On SSDs, RocksDB's sequential pattern has lower write amplification. This is one reason LSM-based databases pair better with flash storage.
segments.thought_prompt: Given SSD write amplification, why might an LSM-tree database be better suited for flash than a B-tree database?

segments.text: SSDs are not just fast disks. They have unique physics that demand understanding. Minimize random small writes to reduce write amplification. Enable TRIM. Choose enterprise SSDs with adequate DWPD for write-heavy workloads. And remember: the difference between a good and bad SSD configuration can be 10x in sustained write throughput.
